newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian scientists cut solar energy costs.
newsitem.headline: Australian scientists cut solar energy costs.

text.p: Australian scientists said on Tuesday they had developed a revolutionary process that could halve the costs of solar energy cells and bring cheap, clean power to the country's outback.

Scientist Andrew Blakers told Reuters the new cheaper cells could be in production within three years, offering a viable alternative to diesel generators in remote Australian areas and communities in small developing nations.
"We are still very much in the research and development phase," said Blakers, of the engineering and information technology faculty at Canberra's Australian National University.
"But with appropriate investment by government and investment bodies we could be in production in three or four years competing vigorously against diesel fuels."

The potential application for the new system was widespread, but it was envisaged that those areas not covered by the electricity grid, which were reliant on the transportation of diesel for their generators, would benefit most.

Other than the initial cost of the new solar system there would ideally be no need for any further financial outlay, particularly since there were no moving parts and no need for maintenance, Blakers said.
The new "epilift" process allowed the cheap production of the most expensive component of solar cells, the silicon wafers.
"Until now, the silicon wafers used by the solar industry have been made in a multi-step process that wastes around 90 percent of the expensive raw silicon," Blakers said.

With the old method, the silicon is decomposed into toxic and corrosive gases which are then condensed and resmelted into large blocks of pure silicon. Thin wafers are then cut off for cell production.
This expensive process accounts for half the cost of the finished solar cell, about A$4 - A$5 (US$3 - US$3.70) per watt.
The epilift technique grows each cell individually in a single step, employing a reusable silicon template and so is more efficient and more cost effective in the long term.

Laboratory trials of templates showed them to have a long reusable life and the group's business manager, Ulrich Theden, told Reuters they would only be vulnerable to direct damage through carelessness.
The epilift invention was now patent-protected and Theden said he would seek financial support from industries to continue research.
The response from companies approached, including the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, has been cautious ao far.
"In Australia, it is almost impossible to get any research money without industry support," Theden said.
"That's our biggest problem. To take our development to the next phase we would probably need A$1 - A$2 million a year for the next three or four years.
"With that money we would have a convicing product which we could hand over to industry to take into production."
